newsitem.title: USA: Clean air group urges utility emissions cap.
newsitem.headline: Clean air group urges utility emissions cap.

text.p: Congress or the Environmental Protection Agency must act soon to adopt a cap on utility emissions and trading rights for the United States to meet its environmental standard targets, the Center for Clean Air Policy said Thursday.

The deregulation of the U.S. utility industry means that older, dirtier, coal-fired plants will have an incentive to increase production, said Ned Helme, director of the group which includes utilities, environmentalists and state governors.
Older, coal-fired plants are usually cheaper to operate, although less efficient, he said.

The group called on the Congress to include an emissions "cap and trade" policy in federal restructuring legislation covering the utility industry. Alternatively, the EPA could act to set ceilings on nitrogen oxide emissions in each state in the eastern half of the nation and create a system of emissions rights trading, Helme said.
"The cost of environmental controls is very small, compared to the savings for consumers from lower rates," said Helme, whose group supports the deregulation of the industry.
In a report released Wednesday, the group studied a pair of representative utilities for a two-year period to gauge the impact of U.S. utility deregulation on clean air quality.

The study estimated that American Electric Power, an Ohio-based utility, would likely increase its nitrogen oxide emissions during ozone season by 25 percent, spewing an additional 53,000 tons into the air. By comparison, the New York Power Pool's utility plants must comply with a statewide cap of 43,000 tons during the same time period.

AEP would also likely boost its emissions of carbon dioxide by up to 30 million tons in 1999, in contrast to the existing U.S. goal of cutting nationwide utility emissions of carbon dioxide by nearly 250 million tons, Helme said.

Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA is preparing to require state caps that may limit utility nitrogen oxide emissions to no more than 1 million tons during the summer ozone season, he said. In the ozone season of 1995, utilities emitted 2.3 million tons of nitrogen oxide.

"Restructuring the electricity market is like building a new house -- if you leave the environment out of the blueprint, it will weaken its foundation, and ultimately the structure will collapse," Helme said.
